Pick the .iso of your own Raging Blast 2 disc (Xbox 360, USA, Rev 1). The app extracts and checks it; you can delete the .iso afterwards. Nothing is uploaded.

The extracted game is removed (about 6 GB). Your saves and settings stay.
How the game screen is held.

Landscape: the phone lying down, the usual way to play (recommended).

Portrait: the phone standing up; the picture sits at the top and the on-screen controller below it, handy for menus and playing with one hand.

Sensor: follows how you hold the phone and turns by itself.
Ko-fi keeps these ports going. Thank you!
Resolution and upscaling in one tap

Renut (default): a native renderer that draws the game\'s Direct3D straight in Vulkan, with no GPU emulation. Much lighter, and it draws from 360p up to 4K. Beta: written for Raging Blast 2 on the same base as Dragon Burst.\n\nXenia: emulates the Xbox 360 GPU (EDRAM, resolves) over Vulkan. Heavier and limited to 720p; kept for comparison, or if something looks wrong in Renut.
Internal size the game draws at.

The size the game draws at. Raging Blast 2 was made for 720p (1280x720). Above it (Renut only: 1080p, 2K, 4K) edges and textures get sharper but the GPU works harder; below it (540p, 480p, 360p) the phone stays cooler and frames steadier, and the upscaler stretches the picture to your screen.

With Renut it changes live from the in-game menu. Xenia goes up to 720p and applies it on reopening.

If frames drop after a few minutes of play the phone is throttling: lower this one step.
How the 16:9 picture fills a wider screen.

Raging Blast 2 draws a 16:9 picture. Phones are wider (20:9 and up).

16:9: the game's own shape, with black bars at the sides.

Stretch: the same picture stretched over the whole screen, a little wider than drawn.

Changes at once, also from the in-game menu.

Saves the logs in a .zip to share (Discord, e-mail).
How the picture is stretched to the screen.

Bilinear: plain and soft, the lightest. Recommended at 720p and above.\n\nFSR 1 (AMD FidelityFX Super Resolution): sharper edges when the game draws well below your screen (540p and lower), for a small GPU cost.

Raging Blast 2 runs its game logic once per frame, so it always plays at 60: capping it at 30 would make the whole game run at half speed.\n\n120 FPS: frame generation adds one interpolated picture between two real ones, for 120 Hz screens. Smoother motion, about one frame more of input delay and more battery.
Shows the frames per second and the frame time in the top corner while you play. Useful to compare settings and drivers.
Stops the game when you leave it.
When you switch to another app or turn the screen off, the game stops drawing and waits: no battery or heat spent on a picture nobody sees. It continues where it was when you come back.
Keeps music and voices on phone speakers.

The game mixes its music and voices on the 5.1 centre channel. Many phones drop that channel and play only effects. With this on the app folds 5.1 to stereo itself, so nothing is lost. Turn it off only on a real surround setup.

Automatic: shown while you play by touch, hidden as soon as a controller is used, and back when you touch the screen again.

Always: always on screen.

Off: controller only.
Ready-made controllers for each way of playing.

Pro: made for competitive play. Dynamic stick that appears under your thumb anywhere on the left side, bigger touch areas on the buttons and sliding between buttons to chain attacks.

Normal: the balanced layout: dynamic stick, buttons in the usual place.

Casual: large fixed stick and buttons; charging and guarding stay held with one tap.

After choosing, fine-tune size, opacity and the rest below.
Dynamic stick that appears under your thumb on the left half, 28% larger touch areas, and sliding between buttons with a guard against accidental slides.
Dynamic stick, slightly enlarged touch areas, one button per touch.
Fixed stick that stays in place, larger touch areas, no sliding between buttons.

Dragon: action icons (punch, ki, guard, dash, Super Attacks...) in the port's own look, with a small badge naming the pad button.

Xbox: A B X Y in their colours, as the game shows them.

PlayStation: cross, circle, square and triangle.

Nintendo: B A Y X in Nintendo's positions.

Only the look changes: each position always does the same action.
Menus always keep the game\'s controls
How the fight buttons are laid out on the screen.

Raging Blast 2: the game's own controls, button by button. The four Super Attacks are on one disc: drag towards a direction to pick one, or just tap it for the first.

Modern: one tap per action, like newer Dragon Ball games. Sway, Vanishing, Counter and Throw (normally Guard + a button) get their own buttons, and so do the Ultimate, ki charge, ascend and descend.

Tenkaichi 3: fights play like Budokai Tenkaichi 3, on the screen and on a physical controller: □ melee, △ ki blast, ○ guard, ✕ dash, R1 / R2 up / down, L2 held charges ki, L2+○ Blast 1, L2+△ Blast 2 (with ↑ → ← the other Super Attacks), L2+↓△ Ultimate, R3 transform. The game reads them as its own moves; menus and the pause menu keep the usual buttons.

Each scheme keeps its own layout in the editor. Menus always use the menu layout.
Drag the buttons · tap one to edit it
All selected buttons are pressed together while you hold.
Steps run in order, 60 frames = 1 second. Forward / Back = towards / away from the opponent.
Macros only send controller buttons: the game sees them as a normal controller.
Fixed: always in the same place; you aim for it.\n\nDynamic: appears wherever your thumb lands on the left side and follows it if you slide past the edge. Fewer missed touches in fast fights.
Small thumb movements near the centre are ignored, so resting the thumb does not move the fighter. Raise it if your character drifts; lower it for finer control.
Chain attacks without lifting the thumb.

Slide your thumb from one face button to a neighbour and the second one is pressed without lifting. To avoid accidents the thumb has to go well inside the next button (past a third of its radius) and stay there for a moment; between buttons there is a neutral band where nothing is pressed, and only neighbouring buttons chain, never across the diamond.
Mirrors the layout: stick on the right.
A short buzz on each press.

On Nintendo-style controllers (Switch Pro, 8BitDo in Switch mode, many handhelds) A and B, X and Y are swapped compared to Xbox. Turn this on so the button in each position does what the game expects there.
What the game loads next time

Automatic: on Adreno the bundled Turnip when this build has it, otherwise the phone's own driver; on Mali and other GPUs the phone's own driver.

A downloaded driver only replaces Vulkan for this game. If it cannot find your GPU, the game falls back to the phone's own driver by itself and this tab shows what really ran.

New driver, odd picture or crash? Go back to Automatic.

What to send when something goes wrong
More lines in the game\'s log.
Writes debug-level lines to the game\'s log (logs/rb2.log). Use it to chase a crash or a graphics problem, then turn it off: it costs a little performance and space.
End of the last game log
GPU time, draws and clock on screen.
Shows GPU time per frame, draw calls, CPU and GPU load and temperature over the game. For testing drivers and settings; turn it off to play.
For testing: one option per line

Options handed to the game\'s runtime when it starts, one per line (for example --vsync=false). They replace the launcher\'s value for the same option. Only for tests asked for in a bug report: a wrong option can stop the game from starting. Clear the box to go back to normal.
After a driver change or odd colours, clearing the cache makes the game rebuild its shaders (the first fights stutter a little).
Every launcher setting goes back to its default. Game files, saves and drivers stay.
Test build: launcher only, without the game engine
Native Android port of Dragon Ball: Raging Blast 2 (Xbox 360). The game\'s PowerPC code is recompiled ahead of time to ARM64 and runs natively, with no emulator, on the ReXGlue runtime over Vulkan.
